# Japanese UI component morph and rhythmic loop

English translation of the archived Japanese prompt by @okapi_fukugyo. The source calls for Japanese interface copy. The translation and original remain separate. The curator did not run the prompt or test the animation.

- [Pinned source](https://github.com/yihui-dev/awesome-opus5-5-videos/blob/92aee2f586ac0715cb3cbcb6384834f98a33383d/prompts/okapi-fukugyo-166351.md)
- [Original post](https://x.com/okapi_fukugyo/status/2103586082336166351)
- [Source repository license](https://github.com/yihui-dev/awesome-opus5-5-videos/blob/92aee2f586ac0715cb3cbcb6384834f98a33383d/LICENSE). Check the terms of any music, artwork, or footage used in production separately.

## Inputs

Ask me for 3 things: the 8–12 UI components that the shape should become (for example, a button, loading indicator, music player, volume slider, on/off switch, tabs, chart, ⌘K search box, or brief notification), whether to use pure black and white or 1 accent color, and a royalty-free track near 120 BPM (120 beats per minute), such as a Mixkit track cleared for commercial use.

## Direction

Create a polished UI animation suitable for a designer portfolio on Dribbble. Keep 1 shape on screen throughout the sequence, with no cuts. Represent each state by changing that shape's size, corner radius, and color. Replace its contents during a brief blur. Have the cursor trigger every change with a click or drag.

Use a warm light-gray background and black-and-white components. Set the interface text in Japanese using Noto Sans JP. Use Geist for Latin letters, numbers, and symbols. Give the motion the natural feel of a spring with only slight overshoot. Zoom to frame each state at full size. Match the last frame to the first so the piece loops.

Avoid bouncy motion, particle bursts, glow, gradients on components, uneven icon strokes, idle beats, and anything that looks like a template.

## Sequence

Use 120 BPM across 7 bars (about 14 seconds), with an event on every beat.

Button → loading indicator → checkmark → iPhone Dynamic Island-style element → music player with a play/pause morph → drag the scrubber to seek → volume slider that stretches like rubber when dragged beyond maximum → on/off switch toggling to the beat → switch thumb becoming a fluid tab indicator → tabs opening into a self-drawing chart with a hover tooltip → fold into ⌘K search → type to filter results → press Enter → brief notification → back to the button.

## Build

1. Deliver 1 HTML file in a square 1440x1440 format. Compute every visual property from time inside `seek(t)`, where `t` specifies the instant to render. Use no CSS transitions, timers, or state carried between frames.
2. Calculate spring motion directly using a closed-form step response. For a value with multiple changes to its target, add the contribution of each change so time alone determines its value.
3. Give the left and right edges of the active tab indicator separate springs. Stretch the leading edge before the trailing edge. Apply the same method to the switch thumb.
4. During a drag, calculate the value directly from the pressed cursor's position. After release, spring back from the position at that instant.
5. Analyze the song with numpy to locate beats. Start on a bar's downbeat and place interaction sounds using their measured peak positions.
6. Render with Playwright. Export 4 subframes per frame and blend them with ffmpeg `tmix` for motion blur at 60fps.
7. Before rendering the whole sequence, export 1 frame per beat. Fix beat alignment, cramped layouts, and readability problems.

## Pitfalls

Keep `will-change` off elements that the camera scales, since it can blur text. Give outgoing and incoming text inside the morphing container separate timing windows so they do not overlap. Match the last frame to the first, including cursor position and velocity, for a clean loop.

## Start

Ask for the inputs first. Show me a beat-by-beat state list before writing code.

The source repository credits @twoclipping. The linked entry holds the English original, author credits, and source and license information for matching entries.

### Inputs

Ask me which 8 to 12 UI states the shape should become, such as a button, loader, player, slider, switch, tabs, chart, command palette, or toast. Ask whether to use pure black and white or a single accent color. Ask for a royalty-free song near 120 BPM, such as a Mixkit track cleared for commercial use.

### Direction

Create polished UI motion at Dribbble quality. Keep the same shape on screen throughout and never cut. Change its dimensions, corner radius, and color, and swap its contents through a brief blur. The cursor should click or drag to drive every change.

Use a warm light-gray canvas, black-and-white controls, and Geist for the interface. Use springs throughout with only slight overshoot. Zoom the camera so each state fills the frame. The last frame matches the first to close the loop.

Avoid bouncy easing, particle bursts, glow, gradients on controls, inconsistent icon strokes, idle pauses, and template-like effects.

### Sequence

Use 120 BPM over 7 bars, with something happening on every beat.

Button → loader → checkmark → Dynamic Island → music player with a play/pause morph → drag the scrubber to seek → volume slider that stretches beyond its maximum → switch toggling to the beat → switch thumb becoming a liquid tab indicator → tabs expanding into a self-drawing chart with a hover tooltip → fold into a ⌘K command palette → type to filter → press Enter → toast → back to the button.

### Build

1. Use one HTML file and a square 1440x1440 frame. Compute the styles from time in `seek(t)`, without CSS transitions, timers, or state carried between frames.
2. Calculate each spring using a closed-form step response. For values with several target changes, add the spring response for every change so the result is a pure function of time.
3. Give the tab indicator's two edges separate springs so the leading edge stretches ahead of the trailing edge. Use the same technique for the switch thumb.
4. Map the value directly to the cursor while it is held down. On release, spring back from the current position.
5. Analyze the song with numpy to build a beat grid and start on a downbeat. Align each UI sound to its measured peak.
6. Render with Playwright. Sample 4 subframes per frame and blend them with ffmpeg `tmix` for motion blur at 60fps.
7. Before the full render, render one frame on every beat and fix timing, crowding, and readability.

### Pitfalls

Leave `will-change` off anything the camera scales, since it can blur text. Give outgoing and incoming text separate timing windows to prevent overlap. Match the opening and closing frames, including cursor position and velocity.

### Start

Ask for the inputs and show a list of states on the beat grid before writing code.

## Production analysis by the curator

### Target effect and sequence

Make it clear that the same component keeps changing its purpose. The cursor provides a visible reason for each change. The action runs from a click that starts the sequence through playback, volume, toggles, information, commands, and a result notification before returning to the opening.

The prompt asks for 8–12 UI states and gives a longer sequence containing actions such as clicks, typing, and drags. Distinguish component states from actions within them and map the chosen states to the beat grid before coding. The source specifies 7 bars without specifying the meter, so a runtime of 14 seconds cannot be assumed.

### Animation approach

Treat container position, dimensions, radius, and color as continuous parameters evaluated by `seek(t)`. Closed-form springs let you sample any instant without rendering the preceding frames first. Add the separate responses when a target changes multiple times.

Stagger the indicator's spring-driven edges and use a spring return after an overdrag. Limit overshoot to a brief settling motion. Time old text out and new text in separately as the container morphs. Put camera zoom and cursor motion on the same timeline as the container.

### Tools and assets

The source specifies one HTML file, Geist, numpy, Playwright, ffmpeg `tmix`, a royalty-free track around 120 BPM, 8–12 user-selected states, and a choice of black and white or an accent color. It leaves Canvas, SVG, GSAP, and the source of UI sound effects open.

Prepare icons with consistent stroke widths and make a copy list for each state. A table relating action, audio peak, and beat can help with sound timing. Check the terms of the selected track separately.

### Production and acceptance checks

1. Collect states, colors, and music and prepare the beat grid. Mark clicks, holds, releases, shape changes, content swaps, and camera zoom so every beat has an event.
2. Build static states and the continuous morph first. Add the player, sliders, tab indicator, and chart. Review sequence, scrubbing, overdrag stretch, hover tooltip, ⌘K filtering, and toast.
3. Check that the controls follow the held cursor and spring from their current position on release.
4. Render one frame per beat and inspect spacing, overlap, beat alignment, and the clarity of scaled text. Inspect adjacent frames around a release or swap to catch brief faults.
5. Blend 4 subframes and output at 60fps. Compare the container, text, cursor position, and cursor velocity across the loop seam.

These are proposed checks for production. This entry has no render results.

### Adaptation

Replace the player, volume control, chart, or command palette with states from your own product. Keep the single morphing container and show user actions before their feedback. Update fonts, accent colors, icon strokes, and copy together. Recheck chart and tooltip space after replacing data. If the music changes, measure the new beats and reschedule events.

### Sequence and states

Analyze the music, choose a 30-second segment beginning on a downbeat, arrange 8–12 continuous states of a single element, introduce a cursor action before each change, and export the result. The source does not name the states or require a loop.

One possible 8-state sequence for a real product is start button → progress → result card → detail panel → chart → filter → confirmation → completion message. Choose the actual states for the product and keep the count within 8–12.

3. Build the continuous morph first, then add content swaps and cursor movement. Look for abrupt element swaps, hard cuts, and cursor actions that occur after the result.

Keep the 30-second format and the causal order of action and response. Replace the states with a real product workflow, choose the project audio, and remeasure its beats and usable segment. - **Target** — Tell a story without dialogue, giving sound an active role in the narrative.
- **Sequence** — Plant a clue in the ambient sound and reveal the change through a sound tied to an action.
- **Timing** — Run for 45 seconds. The source specifies no sound rhythm.
- **Motion** — Use offscreen sound to direct the camera and motivate character reactions.
- **Look** — The source specifies no palette or typography.
- **Tools and assets** — The source specifies no software, characters, or sound effects.
- **Adaptation** — Create a new sound cue sheet whenever you change the story.
- **Checks** — Review the visuals with the sound off, then review the audio without the picture.
- **Open items** — The story and audio are unavailable. The approach is untested.

## Original reusable prompt by the curator

Write a scene without dialogue. Build it around audible clues and visible reactions, then let the sound and the picture reveal the ending together.
